content.title: Big screen film has Ely connection
content.text: ELY – A bit of Ely will be hitting the big screens on Friday when Fox Searchlight Pictures’ film “Wild” debuts. The movie’s star, actress Reese Witherspoon, sports a replica of an Ely Wintergreen Inuit-styled anorak as she re-enacts former Minnesotan Cheryl Strayed’s best-selling memoir of the same title. “Wild” captures the adventures of Strayed’s 1,100-mile solo-hike on the Pacific Crest Trail from the Mojave Desert to Washington State in 1995. The expedition was Strayed’s way of healing herself after going through a divorce, grieving the death of her mother, and suffering destructive drug and sex addictions. Her story of self-discovery and healing was featured in Oprah’s Book Club 2.0 and has topped the New York Times Best Sellers list. During her hike, Strayed packed a black anorak fleece from Ely’s local winter clothing store, Wintergreen. She bought the parka-like Inuit winter jacket a year before her venture and said she still uses it to this day. “I love it still,” Strayed wrote in an email. “(It’s) very warm and cozy and I have lots of great memories of times I wore it.” The owners of Wintergreen, Paul and Sue Schurke, said they first learned of the anorak’s newfound fame when the film’s previews came out at the end of the summer and friends started sending them video clips of Witherspoon wearing the pullover. “It’s such a powerful story about this woman taking off and trekking a thousand miles by herself,” Sue said about the documented journey. “It’s fun to know that (the anorak) was something she brought and didn’t chuck along the way. It was a cherished item.” Sue said she got the idea of sewing anoraks in the early ‘80s while on a North Pole expedition with Will Steger and his team. The Arctic Inuits they encountered were all wearing the warm, hooded parkas, and so, when Sue returned to Minnesota, she started experimenting with her own needle and thread. “My background is Scandinavian, so I wanted my own flare,” she said about creating the Wintergreen anoraks. “I put the two together and started making this anorak with Scandinavian trim.” The unlikely connection to “Wild” comes at a convenient time for the Schurkes as they work to re-open the doors of their winter gear shop after over a year of closure. “It’s slow-going at first – just to get our heads together,” said Sue. “There’re so many details.” Sue said they’re working on training employees, refinishing the inside of the store on East Sheridan Street in downtown Ely, and sewing their popular winter clothing.
